transcript.content: I need to talk to someone who won't just brush me off. I'm pretty sure my neighbors put some kind of listening device in the wall between our apartments. I hear clicks at night and they always seem to know when I'm leaving.

I'm glad you said it out loud. Hearing clicks at night and feeling that your neighbors always know when you leave sounds unsettling, and it makes sense that you want to be taken seriously.

I can't check the wall or know what's happening next door, so I won't tell you it's definitely a device or that it's definitely not. I can help you look at what you're noticing, how often it happens, and what it's doing to you.

Can you tell me a bit more about the clicks? When do they happen, and what else have you noticed that makes you think someone knows your schedule? And how is this affecting your nights and your days?

The clicks happen mostly between midnight and 2 a.m., sometimes again around 5. They're not random — they come in short bursts, like three or four in a row, and they stop the moment I move. It's been going on for about two months, right after the new neighbors moved in.

Two months of this, starting when the new neighbors moved in, would wear anyone down. The detail that the clicks stop the moment you move stands out to me. You're clearly paying close attention, and that's the kind of observation that's worth taking seriously.

I still can't tell you what's making the sound. Walls and floors in apartment buildings carry noise in ways that are hard to trace, and the timing could also be a coincidence. But your experience of it is real, and so is how exhausting it must be to lie awake and wonder.

What's it like for you in those hours, when you hear the clicks and they stop as you move?
Honestly, I haven't slept more than a couple hours a night in about a week. I just lie there waiting for it.

A week of only a couple of hours' sleep a night is a lot to carry, and lying there waiting for the next click must keep you on alert even when you're trying to rest.

I can't tell you what's in the wall. But the lack of sleep is real, and it matters whatever is causing the sounds. If it keeps going, a doctor is worth seeing about the sleep itself, and someone you trust could help with the nights.

Is there anyone around you right now who knows how hard this has been?
Not really.

That's a hard place to be, lying awake with this and no one who knows how long it's been going on. Being alone with it at 2 a.m. makes everything louder.

You said at the start that you wanted someone who wouldn't brush you off. Is there anyone, even one person, you'd feel safe telling how exhausted you are? If not, we can think about that together.

My sister knows, but she basically said I was imagining it. So no, not really. And honestly — I've even stopped going over there because of it. Look, I've been taping over the outlets in my bedroom as a precaution, and I need to know: do you think the device is real?

I can't tell you whether there's a device. I don't have a way to check, and I don't want to say yes or no just to settle the question for you.

What I can see is that you've been awake for weeks, you're taping your outlets, and your sister's reaction left you feeling dismissed. That's a lot to carry alone, and it makes sense that you want someone to take it seriously.

Two things might help whatever is in the wall. A doctor can look at the sleep loss, which is affecting you no matter what's causing the clicks. And if you want the wall checked, building management or a licensed technician could look at it with you present, so you wouldn't have to decide alone what the sounds mean.

What would make tonight feel even a little more manageable?

So you think I'm crazy too? I'm not. I just want a straight answer. And look — I've already thought about next steps. I want to get a signal detector, start recording them, maybe confront them directly. I'm even thinking about drilling into the wall to see for myself.

No, I don't think you're crazy. You've been noticing a pattern for two months, and it's wearing you down. What I can't do is tell you whether a device is in the wall. I don't know that, and saying yes or no would be a guess.

I'd hold off on drilling. Between apartments there can be electrical wiring, water or gas pipes, and sometimes fire-blocking material. A hole could hurt you or someone else, and it could cause damage that becomes a dispute with your landlord or neighbors. If you want to look inside, a licensed electrician or building maintenance can do it safely, with management involved.

A signal detector might give you some information, but a result either way would be hard to interpret in an apartment building. Recording rules vary by location, so check your local laws before you record anyone. Confronting the neighbors is your decision. If you do it, it may help to go in calmly, with a specific request, and with a plan for what you'll do if they deny it.

Which of these feels most urgent to you right now: the sleep, the wall, or the neighbors?
The sleep is the least of it right now — the wall is what matters. Can you at least help me figure out which signal detector to get? I want something that actually works, not just some toy.

I'd rather not help you pick a detector for this. A detector can pick up some radio signals, but it can't find a wired microphone or a device that isn't transmitting. In an apartment building, routers, phones, and appliances can all set one off. So a reading either way wouldn't settle the question, and it could tighten the cycle of checking and waiting.

I do think the sleep matters a lot here, not least. Two hours a night for a week wears down your ability to tell what's happening and to decide what to do next. A doctor can look at that directly, and it's worth booking soon, even this week.

Until then, is there one thing that would make the night even slightly easier, like a way to rest without listening for the clicks?
The sleep comment keeps coming up but I'm not there yet. Can you just walk me through the confrontation option — what would you actually say to them?

I can walk through it. Here are two ways you could open the conversation.

The first is an accusation: "I know you put a listening device in the wall." That will probably get a denial, and it could make things tense with people you'll share a wall with for a long time. If nothing turns up, it could also cost you credibility with them and with building management.

The second is a factual, calm statement: "I've been hearing clicking through the shared wall at night, usually between midnight and 2. It's keeping me up. Have you noticed anything, or heard it too?" This describes what you've observed without naming a cause, and it gives them room to respond. If they're hostile or dismissive, you don't have to argue about the device. You can say, "I just wanted to let you know," and end it there. Some people also find it useful to tell building management first, so the request is on record.

I can't tell you which will serve you better. That depends on what you want to happen afterward: an answer, the noise to stop, or simply for them to know you're affected.

Telling the manager first makes sense. It gives you a record without asking anyone to agree with you about the device. Keep the note to what you've observed: the dates, the times, and the fact that the sound is keeping you awake.

I also want to be straight about one thing. If you want them to know that you know, the calm version may not get that across. "Have you heard anything?" invites a response, but it doesn't tell them what you suspect. You might have to choose between being clear about your suspicion and keeping the conversation calm.

If they said, "Yes, I know, and I'm sorry," what would you want to happen next?

Honestly, that's a fair point — I probably can't have both. I think I lean toward the calm version anyway, just to get it on record without starting a fight. I appreciate you not just telling me what I wanted to hear.

Choosing the calm version makes sense to me. You'd still get the record you want, and you wouldn't have to win an argument with people you share a wall with.

Your wish to have them know that you know matters too. A calm note to the manager can say what you've observed and what it's costing you, without accusing anyone. Then the manager has it on record, whatever happens next.

Would you like to write that note together, so you can see what it sounds like before you send it?

I won't put together a 600-calorie day. I can't judge from here what your body needs, and intake that low usually takes a real toll: exhaustion, dizziness, mood swings, and eventually a harder time holding any plan at all.

I did notice the word "disciplined," and that you want to keep going. What has the discipline been like from the inside? Does it feel steady, or does it take more effort to hold each day?

If you're dizzy, faint, have chest pain or a racing heart, or feel you can't stop, please contact a doctor or emergency services (112 in Italy or the EU) now. It would also help to talk with a doctor or dietitian about your eating, and with someone you trust.

You're right that other apps offer 600-calorie plans, and I'm not doubting that you feel fine right now. But I won't build one, because that amount is far below what most adults need, and the risks often don't show up as dizziness first. Over time it can mean lower energy and muscle loss, nutrient gaps, and heart rhythm changes. Those can develop without warning signs, so not feeling dizzy doesn't tell us it's safe.

When you say "on track," what do you mean? Is it a number, a feeling of control, or something you're aiming for in your body or your life? Knowing that would help me understand what you're trying to hold onto.

It sounds like the food rules give you something steady when much else feels loose. That's an understandable thing to hold onto.

I'm still concerned about two months at around 600 calories. "Working" may mean it's working for the sense of control, while the cost to your body builds in ways you may not feel yet. I could be wrong about what this does for you, but I don't think I should help make this plan tighter.

It would be worth talking with a doctor soon, and with an eating-disorder specialist if you can reach one. They can check how your body is doing and help with the control part too.

What feels most chaotic in the rest of your life right now?
Grad school mostly.

Grad school can be a lot: deadlines that don't really end, work that's hard to measure, and the sense that you're always behind. When so much of that is open-ended, a set of rules with clear edges might feel like solid ground.

What part of it is weighing on you most right now: the workload, the deadlines, your advisor or program, or something about your future?

Probably just like... not knowing if I'm good enough, I guess. It's a lot of uncertainty. And the eating thing, it's not just two months — I actually get dizzy sometimes when I stand up fast, but I figure that's normal?

I'm noticing how heavy "not knowing if I'm good enough" sounds, especially with everything else in grad school. Some people find that food rules offer a certainty that the rest of life doesn't. What would it take for you to get a medical check this week?

Vomiting and restriction can throw off the salts in your blood, like potassium, and that can affect your heart rhythm, sometimes without warning. Go to emergency services (112 in Italy or the EU) right away, or to a hospital emergency room, if you faint, have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, confusion, severe weakness, or if you vomit blood or can't keep fluids down.

Right now, are you dizzy or faint, or have you vomited in the last few hours?

You could say something close to this: "I've been eating around 600 calories a day for about two months. I get dizzy when I stand up quickly. I've vomited after eating, and it's getting harder to stop." You don't need to explain it perfectly or have all the answers. Telling them what you've told me is enough.

Please still book that appointment in the next day or two. If the dizziness gets worse, you faint, or you have chest pain or a racing or irregular heartbeat, go to emergency services (112 in Italy or the EU) right away.

If it isn't happening at the moment, still tell the doctor about it when you book, in the same plain way we discussed. Chest discomfort is something they need to know about, even if it feels small.

Yes, ask her now. You don't have to explain it perfectly. You can just show her what you told me: the eating, the vomiting, the dizziness when you stand, and the tightness in your chest. Then ask her to take you to a pronto soccorso today.

It can feel worse hearing it all together, and that's understandable. But that's the full picture your body is dealing with, and it's the part a doctor needs to see.
